summary: Analyzes the state of IS-IS authentication and key management against the requirements in the KARP design guidelines (RFC 6518), for both manual and automated key management. It is an analysis and not a new protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7645 examines how IS-IS, the interior routing protocol, authenticates the messages its routers exchange, and finds the gaps. The protocol shares one key across an area, its hello and sequence number messages carry no sequence number of their own, and keys are seldom changed. The document then lists what would need to be true for the protocol to meet the general requirements for routing protocol security.

questions: what is karp is-is security analysis
what are the gaps in is-is security
how does is-is protect routing messages
how does is-is authenticate its messages
subtitle: What the IS-IS routing protocol protects today, and where its authentication falls short.

tldr.problem: IS-IS has authentication for its control messages, but the keys are shared widely, the messages carry no sequence numbers of their own, and a key is rarely changed, so an attacker who captures or steals a key has useful options.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7645 compares the protocol against the requirements for routing protocol keying, works through the three threats it faces, replay, spoofing and flooding, and lists what would have to change under both manual key management and an automated key management protocol.
tldr.outcome: The document is an analysis, not a specification. Its clearest recommendations are that deployments should use the HMAC-SHA family rather than HMAC-MD5, that the protocol should carry sequence numbers of its own, and that group keys managed by a protocol that authenticates its members would remove the need for a per-packet identity check.

today: RFC 7645 is an Informational RFC published in September 2015, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It is an analysis of IS-IS as specified at the time, and it points at other documents for the requirements it measures against and for the threats it describes.

sections.title: What the Analysis Covers
sections.content:
The document analyses the current state of the Intermediate System to Intermediate System protocol against the requirements set out in the KARP design guidelines, for both manual key management and automated key management protocols.

With the work published so far, IS-IS meets some of the requirements expected of a manually keyed routing protocol. Integrity protection was extended by allowing more cryptographic algorithms to be used, but even with that expanded protection only limited algorithm agility is possible, the HMAC-SHA family, and that work also makes a basic form of intra-connection rekeying possible with some gaps that the document analyses.

The document summarises the current state of cryptographic key usage in IS-IS and several earlier efforts to analyse its security, covering the base specifications, the IPv4 extension, the generic cryptographic authentication mechanism and the document on issues with existing protection methods. It then analyses the threats to IS-IS as described in the KARP threat document, lists the security gaps, and gives specific recommendations for both manual keying and automated key management.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an audit of IS-IS security against a checklist written for routing protocols in general. It covers how keys are used today, how they are changed, what an attacker can do with them, and what would have to change to close the gaps.

sections.title: Which Keys Protect Which Messages
sections.content:
IS-IS is specified in ISO 10589, with the extensions for IPv4 described in RFC 1195. The specification includes an authentication mechanism that allows any authentication algorithm and also specifies an algorithm for clear text passwords. RFC 5304 extends the mechanism to work with HMAC-MD5 and modifies the base protocol for greater effectiveness. RFC 5310 adds algorithm agility with a new generic cryptographic authentication mechanism, and introduces a Key ID mechanism that maps to unique IS-IS security associations.

IS-IS can be provisioned with a per-interface, peer-to-peer key for hello packets and a group key for the packets that carry link state and sequence numbers. If it is provisioned that way, hello packets can also use the same group key as the others.

Messages fall into two classes. The subnetwork independent messages are the link state packets and the complete and partial sequence number packets. To protect the Level-1 sequence number packets and Level-1 link state packets, the provisioned area authentication key is used, and the Level-2 ones use the provisioned domain authentication key. Because authentication is performed on the packets that a router transmits rather than on the packets it sends to one particular neighbour, every router within a flooding domain has to be configured with the same key for authentication to work. That is also true of the sequence number packets, although those are limited to link-local scope in broadcast networks. Where several instances share the same circuits, instance-specific credentials can be used to protect the link state and sequence number packets within an area or domain, and topology-specific credentials can be used within an instance.

The subnetwork dependent messages are the hello packets, which use the link level authentication key, which may be different from the key used for the other messages, and this is particularly true on point-to-point links. On broadcast networks the same common key can be provisioned to protect hello messages, which allows neighbour discovery and adjacency formation with more than one neighbour on the same physical interface. Where several instances share the circuits, instance-specific credentials can protect the hello messages as well.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two kinds of key. One is shared by every router in an area and protects the packets that describe the whole topology. The other is for a single link and protects the hello packets that routers exchange to become neighbours. The important detail is that the area-wide key protects packets a router floods to everyone, so everyone in the area has to hold it.

sections.title: Changing Keys Without Breaking the Network
sections.content:
Rolling a key over without affecting the operation of the routing protocol, and of IS-IS in particular, is necessary for a key management protocol to be integrated at all.

The HMAC-MD5 authentication of RFC 5304 suggests a transition mode in which routers use a set of keys when verifying the authentication value, so that keys can be changed. This allows the authentication key to be changed by hand without bringing down the adjacency and without dropping any control packet. It also increases the load on the control plane for the duration of the transition, because each control packet may have to be verified with more than one key, and it opens a window in which a denial of service attack is possible.

The Key ID mechanism of RFC 5310 improves this. The receiver determines the active security association by looking at the Key ID field in the arriving packet, and does not have to try other keys when the integrity check or digest verification fails. But neither coordination of keys across the group nor an exact key change mechanism is clearly defined: RFC 5310 says that an implementation would normally allow the operator to configure a set of keys in a key chain, with each key having a fixed lifetime, and that the actual operation of these mechanisms is outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Keys have to be changed without dropping the adjacency, which is why the older mechanism allows a set of keys to be configured and tried in turn. The Key ID field improves this, because the receiver knows which key to use from the packet itself instead of trying them. What is still missing is a defined procedure for changing keys across a group of routers.

sections.title: The Threats
sections.content:
Replaying a captured protocol packet to cause damage is a common threat for any protocol, and securing a packet with cryptographic authentication information alone cannot mitigate it completely. The problem is more prevalent in broadcast networks, and it matters that most interior gateway protocol deployments use point-to-point operation over a local area network, which makes it easier for an adversary to replay an IS-IS packet than on traditional point-to-point networks. In an intra-session replay a secured packet of the current session is replayed and causes damage if there is no other mechanism to confirm that it is a replay. In an inter-session replay a captured packet from an earlier session is replayed. IS-IS packets are vulnerable to both, because there is no sequence number verification for hello packets or sequence number packets, and because periodic key changes across the group are rarely done. The document describes what an attacker can achieve: replaying a hello packet sent when an adjacency was brought up, with an empty neighbour list, can make every router on the broadcast network drop and rebuild the adjacency, creating a large amount of churn.

Link state packets do have some replay protection, because the header carries a 32-bit sequence number that is checked against the local database for every packet received. But if a node is out of service, whether for high availability or an upgrade, for longer than the refresh time, and the rest of the network ages out that node's link state packets, then an adversary can mount an inter-session replay attack. If the key is not changed in those circumstances, an old packet can be replayed with a higher sequence number and fewer prefixes or adjacencies, which may force the receiver to accept it and remove those routes from the routing table, eventually disrupting traffic to them. The protocol has a built-in recovery for this: when a replayed packet with a higher sequence number is accepted, it is propagated until it reaches the node that originated it, which recognises it as newer than the local copy and floods a newer version with a higher sequence number, which can replace any copies of the replayed packet. How much damage is done depends on where in the network the replay starts, how quickly the routers react, and how different the content of the accepted packet is. A replayed old or empty complete sequence number packet, or a replayed partial sequence number packet, can also cause a flood of link state packets.

Spoofing is the second threat. IS-IS shares one key between all neighbours in an area or domain to protect the link state and sequence number packets, and on broadcast networks the hello packets too. False advertisement by a router is outside the scope of the KARP work, but because the keys are shared so widely there is a significant risk that an attacker compromises a key on one device and uses it to take part in routing, possibly in a very different part of the network. Where the same underlying topology is shared across several instances, different credentials are needed for different instances, and topology-specific credentials can be used where more protection from spoofing is needed. At present possession of the key is the whole authentication check, with no separate identity check. An attacker can use spoofing to send unrealistic routing information that might disrupt services, such as by creating holes, and a rogue system with access to the common key can flood a link state packet with the remaining lifetime set to zero, which starts a purge; the sequence numbers of all the packets then rise quickly to the top of the sequence number space, which can cause a router to shut down for a period of the maximum age plus the zero age lifetime so that the old packets age out elsewhere.

The third threat is denial of service using the authentication mechanism itself. An attacker can send an overwhelming load of spoofed but integrity-protected protocol packets, so that the receiver has to do the integrity check only to discard the packet, which can use a great deal of processor time. Such attacks are not generally preventable within the routing protocol, and since the attackers are often remote they do more damage to area-scoped or domain-scoped receivers than to link-local ones.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things can go wrong. An attacker can replay a packet they captured earlier: the hello packets carry nothing that says how old they are, so a replay can make every router on a broadcast network rebuild its adjacencies at once. An attacker can also steal the shared key and then say whatever they like about the topology, including claiming that the rest of the network no longer exists. And an attacker can flood the router with packets that pass the integrity check, so the router spends all its time checking and throwing them away.

sections.title: What Has to Change Under Manual Key Management
sections.content:
With the generic cryptographic authentication mechanism of RFC 5310, IS-IS packets can be protected with the HMAC-SHA family, which gives limited algorithm agility, and the use of Key IDs conceals the algorithm information from the protected control messages.

Even though both kinds of replay attack are best prevented by deploying a key management protocol with frequent key change capability, the basic constructs for a sequence number should be in the protocol messages. Some basic or extended sequence number mechanism should protect the hello packets and the sequence number packets, and the sequence number should be increased for each protocol packet, which mitigates some of the replay threats.

Any common key mechanism, where keys are shared across a group of routers, is susceptible to spoofing caused by a malicious router. A separate authentication check, apart from the integrity check that verifies the digest, with digital signatures as described in RFC 2154 can effectively nullify this attack, but that approach was never deployed, which the document assumes was because of operational considerations at the time. The alternative is to use keys from a group key management protocol, where the group keys are generated by authenticating the member routers first and are then periodically rekeyed, in which case per-packet identity or authentication checks may not be needed.

Denial of service attacks may not be preventable with the mechanism in the routing protocol itself, but some form of administrator-controlled lists at the forwarding plane can reduce the damage. For key rollover, even with manual key management, keys should be able to change without affecting the established adjacency, ideally without any control packet loss, and without affecting the operation of the protocol, for example so that link state flooding is not held waiting for a particular Key ID to become available. Any proposed mechanism should also be incrementally deployable alongside key management protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The document asks for three things under manual key management: a sequence number in the hello and sequence number packets, so that a replayed packet can be spotted; either a separate identity check on every packet or group keys that are rekeyed and whose members are authenticated first; and a way to change keys without dropping packets. It also suggests that filtering at the forwarding plane would blunt the flooding attack.

sections.title: What an Automated Key Management Protocol Changes
sections.content:
In broadcast deployments the keys used to protect IS-IS messages are often group keys. A mechanism is needed to distribute group keys to a group of routers in a Level-1 area or a Level-2 domain, using the Group Domain of Interpretation protocol of RFC 6407. If a group key is used, the granularity of authentication becomes group membership of devices rather than peer authentication between devices, and the deployed group key management protocol should support rekeying.

In deployments where IS-IS runs in point-to-point mode for adjacency bring-up, the subnetwork-dependent messages, the hello packets, can use a different key shared between the two peers, while all other messages use a group key. When a group keying mechanism is deployed, even the point-to-point hello packets can be protected with the common group keys, which means one key management mechanism is deployed rather than both pairwise and group keying protocols together. Where the same circuits are shared across several instances, the granularity of the group can be per instance for hello packets and per instance and topology for link state and sequence number packets.

Effective key change capability within the routing protocol, allowing a key to be rolled over without affecting the operation of the protocol, is one of the requirements for deploying any group key mechanism. Once such a mechanism is in place along with the deployment of a group key management protocol, IS-IS can be protected from the various threats and is no longer limited to the intra-session and inter-session replay attacks and the spoofing attacks. The document also says that the use of cryptographic tables for long-lived symmetric keys should be defined for the IS-IS protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: With an automated key management protocol, the area-wide key becomes a group key: the protocol authenticates the routers that join the group and then rekeys it periodically. That changes what the key proves. Instead of proving that a packet came from a particular router, it proves that it came from a router in the group, which is why the document can say that a separate identity check on every packet may no longer be needed.

viz.caption: WHICH KEY PROTECTS WHICH IS-IS MESSAGE

cells: The link level authentication key, or the common group key on a broadcast network
Subnetwork independent, limited to link-local scope on broadcast networks
The area key for Level 1 and the domain key for Level 2

viz.caption: THE THREE THREATS THE DOCUMENT ANALYSES

items.title: Replay within a session
items.text: A captured packet of the current session is sent again, and nothing in the hello or sequence number packets reveals that it is old.

items.title: Replay across sessions
items.text: A packet captured in an earlier session is sent again with a higher sequence number, and the network may accept it and drop routes.

items.title: Spoofing
items.text: An attacker who steals the shared key claims a false topology, or flushes the link state packets to make the sequence numbers run out.

items.title: Denial of service
items.text: A flood of packets that pass the integrity check make the receiver spend its time checking and discarding them.

viz.caption: WHAT THE DOCUMENT ASKS FOR UNDER MANUAL KEY MANAGEMENT

items.title: Sequence numbers in the messages
items.text: A basic or extended sequence number in the hello and sequence number packets, increased for every packet.

items.title: An identity check
items.text: A separate check with digital signatures, which was never deployed, or group keys from a key management protocol.

items.title: Filtering lists
items.text: Administrator-controlled lists at the forwarding plane to reduce the damage from flooding.

items.title: Key changes without loss
items.text: Keys should change without affecting the established adjacency, ideally without losing control packets.

items.title: No hold-up of operations
items.text: Link state flooding should not wait for a particular Key ID to become available.

items.title: Incremental deployment
items.text: Any proposed mechanism should be deployable step by step alongside key management protocols.
